**Box plus-minus (BPM) estimates a player's contribution in points per 100
possessions from her box score alone: scoring, efficiency, usage, rebounding,
assists, steals, blocks and turnovers.** It cannot see screens, spacing or
defensive positioning, but because box score rates settle quickly it is far more
stable than on/off measures at college sample sizes. `load_wbb_player_value()`
returns offensive, defensive and total BPM for every Division I women's player
since 2014.

This article explains what the model estimates, how it is fitted, how it holds up,
and how to use it responsibly. It condenses the official model card in the
[wehoop-wbb-data repository](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/wehoop-wbb-data/blob/main/docs/models/player_value.md);
numbers quoted from that card are labelled as such.

## What the model estimates

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `box_obpm` | Offensive box plus-minus, points per 100 possessions above average |
| `box_dbpm` | Defensive box plus-minus |
| `box_bpm` | `box_obpm + box_dbpm` |
| `min` | Minutes played |
| `qualified` | `TRUE` when `min >= 300`, the floor below which the estimates are mostly noise |
| `player_id`, `player`, `team_id`, `season` | Identifiers (ESPN ids) |

BPM and RAPM measure different things. RAPM (see the
[women's college RAPM article](womens-college-basketball-rapm-model.html)) sees
everything that happens while a player is on the court but needs many
possessions. BPM sees only the box score but needs few. Treat them as
cross-references, not substitutes.

## Loading the ratings

The ratings are published as Parquet files, so `load_wbb_player_value()` needs
the `arrow` package.

```{r libraries}
library(wehoop)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r load}
pv <- load_wbb_player_value(seasons = 2025:2026)

# Older release files predate the `qualified` flag; derive it the same way.
if (!"qualified" %in% names(pv)) pv$qualified <- pv$min >= 300

pv |> count(season, qualified)
```

Team names come from the box scores, joined on character ids:

```{r names}
team_names <- load_wbb_team_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  transmute(team_id = as.character(team_id), team = team_location) |>
  distinct(team_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

pv <- pv |>
  mutate(team_id = as.character(team_id), player_id = as.character(player_id)) |>
  left_join(team_names, by = "team_id")

pv |>
  filter(season == 2026, qualified) |>
  arrange(desc(box_bpm)) |>
  select(player, team, min, box_obpm, box_dbpm, box_bpm) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  head(15)
```

## Data

As reported in the model card, the inputs are the published player and team
season statistics for women's college basketball, and the team ratings from
`load_wbb_ratings()`. Coverage starts in 2014, the first season with box score
inputs of sufficient quality. The model is recomputed from the current published
data on every run, so upstream corrections flow through on the next publish.

## How the model works

1. **Per-100 features.** Each player's box score is converted to rates per 100
   possessions and shares: points, assists and rebounds per 100, usage, true
   shooting and effective field goal percentage, turnover, steal, block,
   assist and rebound percentages, free throw rate, and shot-location shares.
2. **Standardize.** Each feature is centered and scaled (and clipped at 4
   standard deviations, as reported in the card).
3. **Score.** Separate ridge regressions for offense and defense, fitted at the
   team level, turn the standardized features into raw offensive and defensive
   scores.
4. **Team adjustment.** A uniform adjustment per team makes the team's
   minutes-weighted player scores add up to its adjusted efficiency margin from
   the [team ratings model](womens-college-basketball-team-ratings-model.html).
   This is what anchors BPM to winning.

As reported in the model card, the current coefficients were fitted on the 2025
and 2026 seasons with a ridge penalty of 3.0 for both offense and defense and a
150-minute floor for the team-sum weights. Because every feature is
standardized, a slope is the BPM change for a one-standard-deviation move in
that feature. The largest weights in the card:

| Feature | Offense slope | Defense slope |
|---|---:|---:|
| Points per 100 | 6.932 | -5.442 |
| Usage | -4.567 | 2.661 |
| True shooting % | -0.358 | 1.818 |
| Rebounds per 100 | 0.025 | 1.312 |
| Assists per 100 | 1.112 | -0.877 |
| Turnover % | -0.183 | -0.908 |

The scoring group (points, usage, shooting) carries most of the offensive weight,
and the defensive slopes mirror it with flipped signs. That is the team constraint
at work: offense and defense must add up to one team rating, so a feature that
buys offense is charged against defense. Rebounding and steals are the clearly
defensive contributors. The card reports that the coefficient vector is
published alongside the release as `wbb_player_value_coefficients.json`.

## How well does it work?

### The minutes funnel: why the `qualified` flag exists

The published file keeps every player, including those with a handful of minutes.
With no shrinkage, the most extreme values belong to the smallest samples:

```{r funnel, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of 2025-26 NCAA women's players: minutes played against absolute box plus-minus; extreme values concentrate at low minutes, with a vertical line at 300 minutes."}
pv_2026 <- pv |> filter(season == 2026)

ggplot(pv_2026, aes(min, abs(box_bpm))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, color = "#221A4D") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 300, linetype = "dashed", color = "#b298dc") +
  labs(
    title = "Low-minute players produce the most extreme BPM values",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: the 300-minute qualified floor",
    x = "Minutes", y = "|Box BPM|",
    caption = "Data: wehoop::load_wbb_player_value(seasons = 2026)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r funnel-table}
pv_2026 |>
  mutate(minutes_bin = cut(min, c(0, 50, 100, 200, 300, 600, 800, Inf),
                           include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE)) |>
  group_by(minutes_bin) |>
  summarise(players = n(), sd_box_bpm = sd(box_bpm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

The spread of BPM shrinks as minutes rise and levels off. As reported in the model
card, the 300-minute floor is the first bin whose spread sits within 2% of the
plateau reached at 600 to 800 minutes, measured over all published seasons. Filter
on `qualified` before ranking or comparing players.

### Is it stable from season to season?

A box score model earns its place by persisting for returning players. Here is the
correlation of BPM from 2025 to 2026 for players qualified in both seasons:

```{r yoy}
yoy <- pv |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  select(player_id, season, box_bpm) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = season, values_from = box_bpm,
                     names_prefix = "bpm_", values_fn = mean) |>
  filter(!is.na(bpm_2025), !is.na(bpm_2026))

yoy |> summarise(players = n(), yoy_correlation = cor(bpm_2025, bpm_2026))
```

As reported in the model card, the same check pooled over every published season
pair gives 0.818 over 14,608 player pairs.

### Do offense and defense carry different information?

```{r od}
pv_2026 |>
  filter(qualified) |>
  summarise(players = n(), cor_obpm_dbpm = cor(box_obpm, box_dbpm))
```

A correlation near zero means the two components are not restating each other.

## Reproducing it yourself

- Ratings: `load_wbb_player_value(seasons = ...)` (needs `arrow`), 2014 onward.
- Inputs: `load_wbb_player_box()` for the box scores and `load_wbb_ratings()`
  for the team margins the adjustment uses.
- Method and evaluation in full: the
  [model card](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/wehoop-wbb-data/blob/main/docs/models/player_value.md).

## Limitations

- **The box score is all it sees.** Screening, help defense, spacing and
  defensive attention are invisible, which hurts defensive specialists and helps
  high-volume scorers.
- **No shrinkage.** Low-minute values are unreliable; use the `qualified` flag.
- **Team-anchored.** A player's BPM inherits her team's adjusted margin, so an
  error in the team rating moves the whole roster. As reported in the cards, the
  2015 team ratings are missing, which leaves every 2015 player value empty.
- **Not yet blended with RAPM.** As reported in the card, a hybrid that uses BPM
  as a prior for RAPM is the planned next step.
